name: Boldenone

lead: Boldenone is an injectable anabolic steroid, best known as Equipoise, a veterinary drug for horses. Bodybuilders use it illicitly for steady muscle gain.
No human trials of boldenone were found. Claims about its effects on appearance rest on user reports and a single encyclopedic overview.

paras: It is a testosterone analogue that activates the androgen receptor and is reported to boost red blood cell production. Its long-acting ester releases slowly after injection.
Animal studies report reproductive, liver, kidney and immune effects. It is not approved for humans in the US and is prohibited in sport.

lead: Boldenone is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid (AAS), the 1-dehydro analogue of testosterone. It is used mainly in veterinary medicine, usually as the long-acting undecylenate ester sold as Equipoise, for debilitated horses, and it is not approved for human therapeutic use in the United States.[1]

It is used illicitly by bodybuilders and athletes for steady muscle gain and appetite, and it is a prohibited anabolic agent under anti-doping rules.[1] Human clinical research on boldenone was not found: no trial of it for muscle or appearance appears in the sources reviewed, and information about it comes largely from veterinary use and an AI-generated encyclopedic overview. Evidence for its appearance effects is therefore unproven.
infobox: Veterinary (horses); not approved for humans in the US

paras: In veterinary medicine boldenone undecylenate is given by intramuscular injection to horses to improve weight, appetite and red blood cell production during debilitation from disease or surgery.[1] Illicit human users take it for muscle gain and endurance, with the slow-release ester valued for steady effects.[1]

Boldenone has an extra double bond between carbons 1 and 2 of the steroid A ring relative to testosterone, and is reported to have a higher anabolic-to-androgenic ratio.[1] It acts as an androgen receptor agonist and is reported to stimulate red blood cell production.[1] The undecylenate ester releases slowly over weeks after injection, and metabolites can be detectable in horse urine for months, according to an encyclopedic overview.[1] Human pharmacokinetic data are limited and come from illicit use.[1]

No studies found of boldenone in human clinical trials. Reported research is veterinary and animal, including equine pharmacokinetic work and animal studies describing reproductive toxicity, hepatorenal impairment and immune effects.[1]

Boldenone is on the World Anti-Doping Agency list of prohibited anabolic agents and is reported in roughly 5 percent of global anabolic steroid doping violations, sometimes linked to contaminated meat as well as intentional use.[1]
